title: Reading Your Royalty Statements
metaTitle: How to Read Utah Mineral Royalty Statements
metaDescription: A plain-language walkthrough of the Utah royalty statement: deductions, price codes, decline curves, and what to flag before you decide whether to hold or sell.
heroLead: Most owners we talk with in the Uinta and Paradox basins have a drawer full of royalty stubs they have never really read line by line.
intro: A royalty statement is the one document that tells the truth about what an interest is actually producing, month over month, after the operator's deductions are taken. Families who inherited a fractional interest from a grandparent's allotment often treat the check as the whole story. It isn't. The statement behind the check carries the volume, the price, the deduction code, and the well or unit name — the pieces that let you (or an advisor working for you) judge whether an interest is worth holding, worth leasing again, or worth selling now while activity is visible.

We read statements as part of every conversation with an owner, and we walk through this same breakdown before we ever quote a range. The goal here is to give you the same literacy, whether you sell to us, to someone else, or not at all this year.

sections.heading: The line items that actually matter
paragraphs: Ignore the logo at the top and go straight to five columns: property or well name, production month, gross volume, price per barrel or mcf, and net decimal interest. The net decimal is your ownership fraction after unitization — it is usually a long string like 0.00041237 and it rarely matches the fraction you think you own, because spacing units, pooling, and prior severances all touch it.

Below that sits the deduction section, sometimes labeled 'post-production costs' or 'gathering, processing, transportation.' In the Uinta Basin, where waxy crude has to be heated and trucked or railed to a Salt Lake refinery before it can be sold, these deductions run higher than in basins with pipeline takeaway. That is not a red flag by itself — it is the cost structure of the play — but it is the number you want to track statement over statement to see if it is creeping.

sections.heading: Price codes and why your barrel isn't WTI
paragraphs: Uinta black wax and yellow wax crude sell at a differential to benchmark prices because of the heating, trucking, and refining logistics unique to this basin. A statement showing $8 or more under WTI on a given month is normal for this geology, not a sign you are being shorted. What you want to watch is whether that differential is widening over time relative to nearby wells, which can signal a change in takeaway capacity or refinery demand rather than anything about your specific interest.

For gas interests tied to Paradox Basin or older Uinta Basin gas wells, the same logic applies against a regional gas hub price rather than Henry Hub. Ask for the index name on the statement if it isn't printed plainly — most operators will provide it if you call the owner relations line.

sections.heading: Decline, and what a falling check actually tells you
paragraphs: Oil and gas wells decline. A statement that shows volume falling 20 to 40 percent in year two versus year one off a new horizontal well is typical decline curve behavior, not a problem with your interest. What matters is the shape of the decline after that first steep drop — a well that stabilizes into a long, shallow tail can still support meaningful royalty income for a decade or more, while one that keeps falling sharply may be nearing its economic limit.

This is exactly where a portfolio decision comes in. An interest riding a steep decline curve is worth less to a buyer with each passing quarter, because the buyer is pricing a shrinking future income stream. If you are weighing whether to sell, the trend across your last six to twelve statements tells you more than any single month's check.

sections.heading: Suspense, non-consent, and other flags worth a phone call
paragraphs: Some statements show a line for funds held 'in suspense' — often because of an unresolved title issue, a missing heirship affidavit, or a division order that was never returned. On split-estate and checkerboard state trust land parcels common across the Uinta Basin, where SITLA-managed sections sit interleaved with federal and private minerals, title clean-up can take longer than owners expect, and suspended funds can sit for years until it's resolved. It is worth calling the operator's owner relations department once a year just to ask if anything is being held for your interest.

faqs.question: Why does my net decimal interest look so small?
faqs.answer: Spacing and pooling divide production across every mineral owner in the unit rather than only the acreage directly under the wellbore, so a fractional inherited interest translates into a long decimal. It's normal and doesn't mean your interest is wrong — ask the operator for the unit's pooling order if you want to verify the math.

faqs.question: My statement shows a lower price than what I see quoted in the news. Is that a mistake?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Uinta waxy crude sells at a real, persistent differential to WTI because of the heating and trucking required to move it, and gas often prices off a regional index rather than Henry Hub. Compare your price against prior months on the same statement rather than against a national headline number.

faqs.question: What does a 'suspense' line mean and should I worry?
faqs.answer: It means the operator is holding funds tied to your interest, usually pending a title or heirship document. It is common on older, inherited interests and on parcels with a mixed state-trust and federal history. Call the owner relations line and ask what document is needed to release it.

faqs.question: Can I use my royalty statements when I'm deciding whether to sell?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. Six to twelve months of statements show volume trend, price trend, and deduction trend, which is exactly what a buyer prices when quoting a range. Bring recent statements to any conversation about selling, whether it's with us or another party.
